prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep B019 as a single-achievement prize with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not change my scientific view, and I want to say why unanimity is not what holds it in place. The criterion I would apply to any field is a specific discovery that altered how a process is understood, confirmed independently over time. Proglucagon processing, the incretin effect in humans, the active truncated GLP-1 peptide and its receptor biology meet that test, and the large outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease show that the physiology was correct. The citation I propose credits discoveries of the physiology and of the active form, and states that these made the therapies possible. It does not claim the drugs, and it does not rule on who first isolated which peptide fragment. That wording answers the chair's second question without deciding the Habener question.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses remain attribution and scope. First, if Mojsov's priority for the active peptide could not be defended, the trio would need to change, and I cannot settle that from the supplied record. Second, leaving out Knudsen is a real choice. The long-acting acylated analogues are a scientific advance in their own right, and a reader could say the prize honours the hormone and passes over the medicine. I accept that cost because a three-person cap forces a choice and the physiology is what made the target credible. If the committee decided that the prize should reward translation as much as discovery, my configuration would be the wrong one. Third, adding any second part would force at least one of the three physiologists out, and I do not think that trade improves the prize.

responses.point: She argues that Knudsen's work is arguably as decisive for patients as the physiology, so the exclusion is a contested judgment, and that the citation should say the physiology enabled the therapies rather than claim the drugs. She would take B040 as a second part only if the union stayed within three people, and otherwise keeps B019 alone.
responses.response: I agree with her on the citation, and my wording follows hers: it credits the physiology and the active peptide and says the therapies depended on them. I would go one step further on Knudsen. Her exclusion should be described as a consequence of the cap and of the choice to credit discovery, not as a verdict that the chemistry is minor. Where I differ slightly is on whether Habener's absence from the ballot is only a limit of the ballot. It is, but it also means we are choosing a trio without hearing the strongest competing account, so I would keep Mojsov in only because the supplied record gives no sufficient reason to remove her. On her view that B019 should stand alone if the union has to stay at three, I agree, and that is why my final configuration has one part.

responses.point: He supports the three-name core without Knudsen, says the disputed priority around the active peptide should be stated openly, and treats B040 as the strongest basic-science alternative rather than a competitor to B019. He ranks B030 only fifth and prefers Hall with Schreiber for TOR.
responses.response: I accept his point that the Mojsov question is a weakness of the academic trio that we should acknowledge in discussion, and I do so here. We agree that B040 is an alternative and not a rival to B019, and his reading of the Ire1, Hac1 and XBP1 mechanism as clean matches mine. I still rank B030 above where he does, because the haematologic response is unambiguous, replicated and created a new class of therapy, although I concede that Eshhar's absence leaves the credit less settled than for B040. On TOR I have kept it out of my configuration. His preference for Hall with Schreiber and mine for Hall alone are both defensible, but with the 2026 list already containing B019 and no second part I am proposing, we do not need to resolve it now.

responses.point: As chair he places B040 fourth and sees its disease link as mostly mechanistic, with no therapy yet. He keeps B030 as his first alternative and B012 second, and says the evidence supplied is not enough to drop the discovery trio.
responses.response: I agree that no evidence supplied justifies dropping the trio. On B040 our difference is narrower than it looks. I accept that the absence of a therapy is a weakness for a Medicine prize and that it matters more than I gave it credit for in round 1, which is a reason why I put it as an alternative to B019 and not as a partner for it. It would be a stronger second choice than B030 only if the committee prefers a clean pair of names to a larger clinical effect with unsettled credit. I think that preference is reasonable but not compelling, and I would not defend it as strongly as I did in round 1. On B012 I note his view that the tool has changed experimental physiology. I still see six names for three places, with no trio that leaves out none of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck, so I would not support it this year.

responses.point: He answered my sixth-place ranking of B012 by saying causal circuit control has changed physiology across neural, cardiac and retinal systems, and that vision restoration is reaching patients. He accepts the six-name allocation problem and would not put it ahead of GLP-1.
responses.response: I take his point that vision restoration and cardiac applications are moving beyond a pure research tool, and I would now put B012 somewhat higher than sixth on medical relevance than I did. That is a limited change. The allocation problem is not softened by clinical progress: Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel is the trio most colleagues name, yet Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck have claims that a committee would have to explain, and I do not think this year's prize should require us to explain that. His own conclusion, that B012 is a serious second but not ahead of GLP-1, is where I end up. I did not move it into my alternatives because B040 and B030 each have a clearer two or three name allocation.

uncertainties: Whether the priority of the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide, Mojsov against Habener's group, holds up. I cannot verify it from the supplied record, and my configuration depends on it.
Whether the committee wants the citation to cover the long-acting analogue step. If so, Knudsen would replace one of the three, and I would not know which.
Whether the second choice, if the committee ever wanted a second part, should be a clean mechanistic pair (B040) or a clinically stronger candidate with unsettled credit (B030).
Long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy, including effects in pregnancy and young patients, which are still accumulating but do not change the core discovery.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I co-authored nuclear-receptor work with Ronald Evans and have collaborated with Per Svenningsson and Johan Ericson, mainly on dopamine-neuron topics. None of these people is credited on any shortlisted ballot, so I request no recusal. I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Mori, Walter, June, Sadelain or Rosenberg.
